subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Dunning-Kruger Effect
description: A 60-second lesson on The Dunning-Kruger Effect.

hook.text: A man robs a bank with lemon juice on his face, sure it makes him invisible to cameras. He was arrested quickly.

buildup.text: Dunning and Kruger found that the least competent people overestimate their skill the most.

discovery.text: The problem: the skills needed to be good at something are the same skills needed to judge your ability.

twist.text: Experts make the opposite error—they assume others know what they know and underrate their own skills.

climax.text: The cure is feedback and metacognition. Once beginners learn the skill, they recognize their past errors.

punchline.text: You need skill to know you lack skill.

quiz.question: What drives the Dunning-Kruger effect?
options: Lacking the skills to evaluate one's own competence

details.summary: The Dunning-Kruger effect describes how people with limited knowledge in a domain tend to overestimate their competence, while experts tend to underestimate theirs. The same skills needed to produce correct answers are needed to recognize correct answers, creating a double curse for beginners.
details.whyItMatters: The Dunning-Kruger effect explains why overconfident amateurs make poor decisions and why experts hesitate. It has implications for education, hiring, and public discourse.
takeaways: Low performers tend to overestimate their abilities
Experts tend to slightly underestimate their competence
Metacognitive skills improve with genuine expertise

faq.question: Is the Dunning-Kruger effect supported by solid research?
faq.answer: The original finding is well replicated: poor performers overestimate themselves. Recent critiques argue that statistical artifacts partly explain the pattern. However, the core insight that incompetence limits self-assessment remains supported by multiple lines of evidence.

faq.question: How can someone detect the Dunning-Kruger effect in themselves?
faq.answer: Seek honest feedback from knowledgeable people. Compare your predictions with outcomes. Learn enough about a field to recognize what you do not know. The effect diminishes with genuine learning because increased knowledge improves the ability to judge your own performance.
